'''William W. Warner''' (April 2, 1920 – April 18, 2008)<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/30/books/30warner.html Obituary] in ''[[The New York Times]]''.</ref><ref name=Holley>{{Citation | first = Joe | last = Holley | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/04/29/AR2008042902935.html  | title = William Warner; Wrote Classic On Chesapeake | page = Obituaries |  newspaper = The Washington Post | location = Washington, D.C | date = April 30, 2008 }}</ref> was an American [[biologist]] and writer. He was awarded the 1977 [[Pulitzer Prize]] for General Nonfiction for his first book ''[[Beautiful Swimmers: Watermen, Crabs and the Chesapeake Bay]]'', which was based on his experiences living and working among crab fishermen on the [[Chesapeake Bay|Chesapeake]].

Warner was a 1943 graduate of [[Princeton University]].<ref name=Holley/> During World War II, Warner served in the [[Pacific Ocean theatre of World War II|Pacific Theater of operations]] as an aerial photograph analyst with a [[United States Marine Corps|Marine]] air group.<ref name=Holley/>

==Works==
* ''[[Beautiful Swimmers: Watermen, Crabs, and the Chesapeake Bay]]'' (1976)
* ''Distant Water: The Fate of the North Atlantic Fisherman'' (1983)
* ''Into the Porcupine Cave and Other Odysseys: Adventures of an Occasional Naturalist'' (1999, short stories)
* ''At Peace with All Their Neighbors: Catholics and Catholicism in the National Capital, 1787–1860'' (1994)
